title: Fundamental Rights and Fundamental Duties
summary: Rights are claims of an individual that are essential for his or her development and are recognised by society or the State. A duty is something one is expected or required to do. Rights and duties are 'two wheels of the chariot of life': my right brings an obligation to respect the same right of others — if I have the right to use a public park, it is my duty not to deny it to others.

The most important rights are written in the Constitution and are justiciable — enforceable through courts; a law that violates them can be declared invalid. Originally there were seven; the Right to Property was removed in 1978 by the 44th Amendment and is now only a legal right. Today there are six.

1. Right to Equality (Articles 14–18): equality before law; no discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth (special provisions allowed for women and children); equality of opportunity in public employment (with reservation for SC, ST and OBC); abolition of untouchability — practising it in any form is a punishable offence; abolition of titles like 'Sir' and 'Rai Bahadur' (national awards such as Bharat Ratna, Padma awards and gallantry awards are not titles).

2. Right to Freedom (Articles 19–22): Article 19 gives six freedoms — speech and expression; to assemble peacefully without arms; to form associations and unions; to move freely throughout India; to reside and settle anywhere in India; to practise any profession, trade or business. The State may impose reasonable restrictions in the interest of the sovereignty, integrity and security of India, public order, decency, morality, friendly relations with foreign states, or to prevent contempt of court, defamation and incitement; only courts decide what is reasonable. Article 20: protection in respect of conviction (no punishment for an act that was not an offence then, no double punishment, no forced self-incrimination). Article 21: no one can be deprived of life or personal liberty except by procedure established by law. Article 22: an arrested person must be told the grounds, may consult a lawyer and must be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours (except under preventive detention).

3. Right against Exploitation (Articles 23–24): traffic in human beings (buying and selling people), begar (forced labour without payment) and other forced labour are prohibited and punishable; no child below 14 may be employed in factories, mines or hazardous work.

4. Right to Freedom of Religion (Articles 25–28): India is a secular state with no religion of its own. Everyone has freedom of conscience and to profess, practise and propagate religion — but not to convert by force or allurement, and inhuman practices like sati are banned; restrictions for public order, morality and health. Religious groups may set up institutions, manage their own affairs and own property. No one can be forced to pay taxes for promoting a particular religion. No religious instruction in institutions wholly maintained by the State, and no one can be compelled to attend it elsewhere.

5. Cultural and Educational Rights (Articles 29–30): any minority with a distinct language, script or culture may conserve it; no one can be denied admission to a State-aided institution on grounds of religion, race, caste or language; minorities (religious or linguistic, at national or state level) may establish and run educational institutions and must not be discriminated against in grants.

6. Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32): if any fundamental right is violated, a citizen can directly approach the Supreme Court, which can issue directions, orders and writs. Dr. Ambedkar called it the heart and soul of the Constitution, because it makes all other rights real.

Right to Education: Article 21A was added in 2002 by the 86th Amendment, making free and compulsory education for children of 6–14 years a fundamental right; it became enforceable with the Right to Education Act, 2009.

The UN General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948 (equality before law, life, liberty, free movement, education, freedom of religion, assembly and so on). Many of these are Fundamental Rights in our Constitution; others are in the Directive Principles. The National Human Rights Commission was set up in 1993 to protect human rights in India. Human rights are universal, fundamental and absolute.

The original Constitution had no duties. Ten Fundamental Duties were added in 1976 by the 42nd Amendment: (1) abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals, institutions, the National Flag and National Anthem; (2) cherish the noble ideals of the freedom struggle; (3) uphold the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India; (4) defend the country and render national service; (5) promote harmony and brotherhood and renounce practices derogatory to women; (6) value our composite culture; (7) protect the natural environment — forests, lakes, rivers and wildlife; (8) develop scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry; (9) safeguard public property and abjure violence; (10) strive for excellence. An eleventh duty was added after the RTE Act: parents and guardians must provide education to children of 6–14 years. Duties are non-justiciable — not enforceable by courts — and act as a code of conduct; some are vague.

vsa: Under which Article was the Right to Education included in the Fundamental Rights, and why?

The Right to Education is added by introducing a new Article 21A in the Chapter on Fundamental Rights in 2002 by the 86th Constitutional Amendment. It was a long standing demand so that all children in the age group of 6-14 years (and their parents) can claim compulsory and free education as a Fundamental Right. It is a major step forward in making the country free of illiteracy.
